title: Leaders Don’t Tell Jokes
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The author distinguishes jokes, which make fun of people and events and risk offending someone with each telling, from humorous stories, which build rapport. Good leaders avoid jokes because the downside of demeaning or insulting anyone is never worth the laugh, yet they still value humor. His recommendation is to tell self-effacing stories about personal missteps, parenting, embarrassments or incompetence, which make the leader human. Such stories require confidence and self-security, and they let others see a side of the leader they do not normally see. The post's rule is to look inward at yourself to create a smile rather than feed an inner stand-up comedian.
points: Jokes get retold and the odds they offend someone rise with each telling, so leaders skip them.
Humorous stories, especially self-deprecating ones, build rapport and make leaders human.
Telling a story about your own pratfall takes confidence and self-security.
The path to laughter can easily slide into insult or ridicule, so the safest target is the leader.
quotes: Jokes make fun of people and events. They get retold because the surprise they contain usually confirms a bias or hidden truth. But invariably, someone on the receiving end of the joke doesn’t hold the bias or see the truth. To make matters worse, they often see themselves in the people or events at the brunt of the derision. The odds a joke won’t offend someone goes down with every telling.

Good leaders avoid telling jokes. They understand the downside of offending, demeaning, or insulting others is never worth the laugh. Yet, they also understand and appreciate the power of humor. So, they tell humorous stories instead.

Personal and funny stories are both genuine and engaging. They help leaders to build rapport and connection with others. Better yet, because they are almost always self-effacing, they make leaders human.

Telling a humorous story about a personal pratfall or misstep requires confidence and self-security. When leaders take the chance to inject humor into a conversation or presentation, they are viewed as sharing a part of themselves that others don’t normally see.

Stories of personal frustration, surprise, parenting, prized possessions, embarrassments, lack of ability, overestimation, and incompetence make for great humor. Poking fun at yourself always gets the best laugh.
Rather than feed their inner stand-up comedian, leaders look inward at themselves to create a smile. Listen to authentic leaders and you will learn there is always much to smile about.
